sec06-card-r45.expected_back: For a reverse two-point turn, signal right, stop and check beside and behind the vehicle before backing toward the driveway.

sec06-card-r46.front: While backing slowly for a reverse two-point turn, when do you start turning the wheel rightward into the driveway?
sec06-card-r46.expected_back: In the reverse two-point procedure, start the rightward backing turn when the rear bumper reaches the driveway's near edge.

sec06-card-r47.front: Once centered inside the driveway on a reverse two-point turn, how do you finish re-entering the road?
sec06-card-r47.expected_back: When centered in the driveway during a reverse two-point turn, straighten the wheels and stop; select drive, check both ways and turn left only when clear after signaling.

sec06-card-r48.front: How do you position, signal, and pull into a driveway or alley for a forward two-point turn?
sec06-card-r48.expected_back: For a forward two-point turn, check mirrors, signal left and turn from near the road center into the right side of the driveway or alley.

sec06-card-r49.front: In a forward two-point turn, where do you stop inside the driveway and which signal goes on before reversing?
sec06-card-r49.expected_back: In a forward two-point turn, stop after the rear clears the road edge; check all directions, signal right and select reverse.

sec06-card-r50.front: How do you steer out of a forward two-point driveway turn and get moving forward again?
sec06-card-r50.expected_back: Back slowly out of the forward two-point setup only with a clear path, steering right; once centered in the nearest lane, straighten, stop, select drive and cancel the signal.

sec06-card-r51.front: Which turnaround does the Kansas handbook warn is the hardest and most dangerous, and when is it allowed?
sec06-card-r51.expected_back: The handbook calls the three-point turnabout its most difficult and dangerous reversal; use it only on a two-lane road too narrow for a U-turn when circling the block is impossible.

sec06-card-r52.front: How do you set up at the right edge of the road to begin a three-point turn?
sec06-card-r52.expected_back: Begin a three-point turn by checking mirrors, signaling right and stopping at the road's right side.

sec06-card-r53.front: What signal, checks, and wheel turn carry you across the road on the first leg of a three-point turn?
sec06-card-r53.expected_back: For the first crossing of a three-point turn, signal left and check traffic and the left blind spot; when clear, steer hard left and stop across the road.

sec06-card-r54.front: On the middle backing leg of a three-point turn, what checks and wheel direction do you use?
sec06-card-r54.expected_back: For the reverse leg of a three-point turn, check traffic and both blind spots; when clear, reverse with a hard right turn and stop.

sec06-card-r55.front: How do you complete the third forward leg of a three-point turnabout?
sec06-card-r55.expected_back: For the final leg of a three-point turn, select drive, signal left and check traffic and blind spots; when clear, turn left into the new direction's right lane and ensure signal cancellation.

sec06-card-r56.front: What two basic conditions determine whether you can legally make a U-turn?
sec06-card-r56.expected_back: U-turns need sufficient turning room and are not permitted everywhere; obey signs prohibiting them.

sec06-card-r57.front: Before swinging a permitted U-turn, what traffic gap and cross-street movement must you watch?
sec06-card-r57.expected_back: Before a permitted U-turn, wait for a large gap in both directions and watch vehicles turning right into the intended path.

sec06-card-r58.front: Which way does traffic circulate around a roundabout island, and who yields at entry?
sec06-card-r58.expected_back: Roundabout traffic moves counterclockwise around a raised island, and entering vehicles yield to circulating traffic.

sec06-card-r59.front: What target speed range does the Kansas handbook recommend when entering a roundabout?
sec06-card-r59.memory_hook: Fifteen to twenty miles per hour
sec06-card-r59.expected_back: The handbook recommends slowing to about fifteen to twenty miles per hour for the sharp curve at roundabout entry.

sec06-card-r60.front: When do you pick your lane for a multilane roundabout, and what two moves are banned inside the circle?
sec06-card-r60.expected_back: Choose the correct roundabout lane before entry, follow signs and markings to the exit, and do not change lanes or pass inside.

sec06-card-r61.front: Who must you yield to at roundabout approaches, including when two vehicles arrive together?
sec06-card-r61.expected_back: Yield to roundabout pedestrians and cyclists; the handbook also tells simultaneous arrivals to yield to a vehicle on the right.

sec06-card-r62.front: Which direction do you steer as you enter a roundabout?
sec06-card-r62.expected_back: Enter the circle to the right and then follow its counterclockwise path.

sec06-card-r63.front: How should you use your turn signal when taking an immediate right turn at a roundabout?
sec06-card-r63.expected_back: For a rightward roundabout movement, signal right on approach and keep signaling until after the exit.

sec06-card-r64.front: How do you signal when going straight through a roundabout?
sec06-card-r64.expected_back: For a straight-through roundabout movement, no approach signal is needed; signal right before the chosen exit.

sec06-card-r65.front: When making a three-quarter left-turn movement around a roundabout, when does the handbook tell you to signal right?
sec06-card-r65.expected_back: For a leftward roundabout movement, the handbook directs a right signal after traveling three quarters around, to take the exit.

sec06-card-r66.front: How should you space your car around semi-trucks or buses inside a roundabout?
sec06-card-r66.expected_back: Avoid driving alongside trucks or buses in a roundabout.

sec06-card-r67.front: Which visual equipment on a stopped school bus requires approaching drivers to stop?
sec06-card-r67.expected_back: Stop for a stopped school bus displaying flashing red lights, an extended stop arm, or both.

sec06-card-r68.front: After school-bus red lights go dark and the stop arm folds in, what else must you confirm before rolling?
sec06-card-r68.expected_back: After the bus lights stop flashing and the arm is withdrawn, proceed only when safe and children have completely cleared the roadway.

sec06-card-r69.front: Do double solid yellow center lines excuse oncoming traffic from stopping for a school bus?
sec06-card-r69.expected_back: Two solid yellow lines do not exempt opposite-direction traffic from the school-bus stopping rule.

sec06-card-r70.front: Does a painted shared center left-turn lane exempt oncoming drivers from stopping for a school bus?
sec06-card-r70.expected_back: A center turning lane does not create an opposite-direction exemption from the school-bus stopping rule.

sec06-card-r71.front: On undivided multilane highways and intersections, which sides of the road must stop for a flashing school bus?
sec06-card-r71.expected_back: The handbook's school-bus stopping examples include multilane highways and intersections for vehicles on either side of the road.

sec06-card-r72.front: When is oncoming traffic NOT required to stop for a school bus flashing red lights?
sec06-card-r72.expected_back: An oncoming school bus does not require a stop when a median or another physical barrier separates the roadways.

sec06-card-r73.front: What two basic safety checks make a roadside parking spot safe for passing traffic?
sec06-card-r73.expected_back: Park where the vehicle will not interfere with a travel lane and can be seen by traffic approaching from either direction.

sec06-card-r74.front: Where should you position your vehicle relative to designated areas, live traffic, and curbs?
sec06-card-r74.expected_back: Use designated parking areas where required and park as far from traffic as possible, close to a curb when present.

sec06-card-r75.front: After setting the parking brake, which gear position secures a manual car versus an automatic car?
sec06-card-r75.expected_back: When parking, set the parking brake, then leave a manual transmission in gear or an automatic in park.

sec06-card-r76.front: What two things should you switch off before removing the ignition key?
sec06-card-r76.expected_back: Switch off headlights and the engine before taking out the key.

sec06-card-r77.front: How do you prevent 'dooring' a cyclist or passing car when exiting a street-parked vehicle?
sec06-card-r77.expected_back: Check mirrors and traffic before opening a vehicle door, and close the door promptly after exiting.

sec06-card-r78.front: What must you always do with your keys and door locks whenever walking away from a parked car?
sec06-card-r78.expected_back: Do not leave ignition keys in a parked vehicle; lock the doors when leaving it.

sec06-card-r79.front: From which end of a street-parked car should you walk toward your driver door, and why?
sec06-card-r79.expected_back: To enter a vehicle parked on a street, approach its driver door from the front with the key ready so oncoming traffic is easier to observe.

sec06-card-r80.front: How close to the curb or road edge should you stop parallel before setting downhill parking wheels?
sec06-card-r80.expected_back: For downhill parking with or without a curb, stop parallel within twelve inches of the curb or road edge.

sec06-card-r81.front: Which way do you turn your front wheels when parking downhill, whether a curb is present or not?
sec06-card-r81.expected_back: For downhill parking, turn the wheels toward the curb or edge while creeping forward and stop as the tire touches the curb or reaches the edge.

sec06-card-r82.front: Which way do you turn your front wheels when parking uphill beside a raised curb?
sec06-card-r82.expected_back: For uphill parking with a curb, stop parallel within twelve inches and turn the wheels away from the curb while moving slowly forward.

sec06-card-r83.front: After turning your wheels away from an uphill curb, how do you seat the tire against the concrete?
sec06-card-r83.expected_back: After setting uphill-with-curb wheel direction, stop and allow a slow roll back until the tire meets the curb, then stop.

sec06-card-r84.front: Which way do you turn your front wheels when parking uphill where there is NO curb?
sec06-card-r84.expected_back: For uphill parking without a curb, stop parallel within twelve inches of the edge and turn toward the edge while creeping forward until the nearest tire reaches it.

sec06-card-r85.front: How should you position your car in a parking aisle before swinging into an angle or perpendicular stall?
sec06-card-r85.expected_back: Before angle or perpendicular parking, identify the space, check traffic, signal and position away from the space to prepare the turn.

sec06-card-r86.front: How should your wheels and car sit once parked inside an angle or ninety-degree stall?
sec06-card-r86.expected_back: Enter an angle or perpendicular space slowly, center the vehicle, straighten the wheels, move to the front and secure it after stopping.

sec06-card-r87.front: What four steps come right before releasing the brake to back out of an angle or perpendicular space?
sec06-card-r87.expected_back: Before backing out of an angle or perpendicular space, check traffic in every direction, hold the brake, select reverse and signal the turn.

sec06-card-r88.front: While backing out of a parking stall, when do you stop and shift into drive?
sec06-card-r88.expected_back: During the parking-space exit, continue checking traffic and back toward the intended rearward direction; stop when centered in the lane before selecting drive.

sec06-card-r100.front: How many feet must parked cars stay from a fire-station driveway on the same side versus across the street?
sec06-card-r100.expected_back: Keep parked vehicles at least twenty feet from a fire-station driveway on the same street side and seventy-five feet from one on the opposite side.

sec06-card-r101.front: Besides driveways, alleys, and private roads, what sidewalk feature must you never block when parking?
sec06-card-r101.expected_back: Do not block a driveway, alley, private road or curb opening lowered for sidewalk access.

sec06-card-r102.front: Which four elevated, recessed, or enclosed road structures prohibit parking completely?
sec06-card-r102.expected_back: Parking is prohibited on bridges, overpasses, underpasses and in tunnels.

sec06-card-r103.front: May you cross oncoming traffic to park facing against the direction of traffic on that curb?
sec06-card-r103.expected_back: Do not park facing against the street's traffic flow.

sec06-card-r104.front: What three forms of official credential allow parking in a marked disability space in Kansas?
sec06-card-r104.expected_back: A marked disability space requires an appropriate disability plate, tag or sticker.

sec06-card-r105.front: Is stopping or parking alongside another curb-parked car in the street lane ever allowed?
sec06-card-r105.expected_back: Do not park beside another parked vehicle on the roadway, or where a sign prohibits parking.

sec06-card-r89.front: Where do you pull up and stop first when setting up to parallel park, and how do you handle cars behind you?
sec06-card-r89.expected_back: Before parallel parking, check traffic and signal; let following traffic pass while stopped beside the vehicle ahead of the chosen space.

sec06-card-r90.front: Once traffic clears, how do you steer backward into a parallel-parking space?
sec06-card-r90.expected_back: With traffic clear, parallel-park by looking in the rearward path and backing slowly, first angling into the space then steering to center the vehicle.

sec06-card-r91.front: How do you finish positioning your car inside a parallel space without tapping the car behind?
sec06-card-r91.expected_back: During parallel parking, stop short of the rear vehicle's bumper, then select drive to adjust the final position.

sec06-card-r92.front: What first move gives your front bumper room to clear the car ahead when leaving a tight parallel spot?
sec06-card-r92.expected_back: Before leaving parallel parking, check traffic, use the brake and reverse carefully toward the vehicle behind to gain room.

sec06-card-r93.front: What checks and clearance check must you make as you pull out of a parallel space into live traffic?
sec06-card-r93.expected_back: To leave parallel parking, check and signal before moving forward slowly into traffic, ensuring the front bumper clears the vehicle ahead.

sec06-card-r94.front: Which four everyday pedestrian and traffic zones forbid parking?
sec06-card-r94.expected_back: Do not park in an intersection, on a crosswalk or sidewalk, or in a construction area where the vehicle blocks traffic.

sec06-card-r95.front: How close to a stop sign, yield sign, or traffic signal does Kansas forbid parking?
sec06-card-r95.expected_back: The handbook prohibits parking within thirty feet of a traffic signal, stop sign or yield sign.

sec06-card-r96.front: How many feet must a parked vehicle stay clear of a pedestrian safety zone?
sec06-card-r96.expected_back: Do not park within thirty feet of a pedestrian safety zone.

sec06-card-r97.front: How close to a fire hydrant is parking prohibited in Kansas?
sec06-card-r97.expected_back: Do not park within fifteen feet of a fire hydrant.

sec06-card-r98.front: Within how many feet of a highway-railroad crossing is parking prohibited?
sec06-card-r98.expected_back: Do not park within fifty feet of a highway-railroad crossing.

sec06-card-r99.front: What is the maximum distance your tires may sit out from the curb when parallel parked?
sec06-card-r99.expected_back: Do not park more than one foot from the curb.

sec06-card-r106.front: What parking rule does a white painted curb indicate?
sec06-card-r106.expected_back: A white painted curb permits short stops only.

sec06-card-r107.front: What restriction does a yellow painted curb identify?
sec06-card-r107.expected_back: A yellow painted curb marks a loading zone or another restriction.

sec06-card-r108.front: Who is a blue painted curb reserved for?
sec06-card-r108.expected_back: A blue painted curb identifies a disability restriction.

sec06-card-r109.front: What strict restriction does a red painted curb mark?
sec06-card-r109.expected_back: A red painted curb identifies fire-zone restrictions.

sec07-card-f01.front: What two hands-on learning pieces can a driver handbook never replace?
sec07-card-f01.expected_back: A handbook cannot replace driving instruction and supervised practice needed to develop experience and judgment.

sec07-card-f02.front: Which three areas around your vehicle must you scan to spot speed or lane problems early?
sec07-card-f02.expected_back: Scan ahead, beside and behind the vehicle to detect problems that may require a speed or position change.

sec07-card-f03.front: How does aiming your eyes far down your intended path improve steering and traffic flow?
sec07-card-f03.expected_back: Looking far along the intended path can reduce emergency reactions and steering weave while helping traffic flow steadily.

sec07-card-f04.front: At least how far ahead does the Kansas handbook recommend looking on a highway?
sec07-card-f04.expected_back: On a highway, the handbook recommends looking at least a quarter-mile ahead.

sec07-card-f05.front: Which ahead-of-you clues let you adjust speed or change lanes well in advance?
sec07-card-f05.expected_back: Search ahead for entering or turning vehicles and brake lights so speed or lane changes can be made early.

sec07-card-f06.front: How should you approach a traffic light that has already been green for a long time?
sec07-card-f06.expected_back: A light that has remained green for a long time may change before arrival; begin slowing and prepare to stop.

sec07-card-f07.front: How do early speed or lane adjustments help drivers following behind you?
sec07-card-f07.expected_back: Early driving adjustments give following drivers more time to respond.

sec07-card-f08.front: How do you measure your look-ahead time while driving?
sec07-card-f08.expected_back: Measure look-ahead time by counting seconds until reaching a stationary object first seen ahead.

sec07-card-f09.front: How many seconds ahead of the vehicle define the Kansas handbook's visual lead?
sec07-card-f09.expected_back: The handbook defines visual lead as the area about twenty to thirty seconds in front of the vehicle.

sec07-card-f10.front: What two survival advantages does a strong twenty-to-thirty-second visual lead provide?
sec07-card-f10.expected_back: A useful visual lead helps identify changing conditions and alternative paths early enough to stop or steer.

sec07-card-f11.front: About how many seconds and feet does the handbook's sixty-mph dry-road stop take?
sec07-card-f11.expected_back: With good tires and brakes on dry pavement, the handbook's sixty miles per hour example allows about four to five seconds or three hundred fifty-nine feet to react and stop.

sec07-card-f12.front: About how many seconds and feet does the handbook's thirty-mph dry-road stop require?
sec07-card-f12.expected_back: Under the same stated good-tire, good-brake and dry-road conditions, its thirty miles per hour example allows about two to three seconds or one hundred twenty-three feet to react and stop.

sec07-card-f13.front: Below what forward visibility distance does the handbook warn sixty miles per hour is too fast?
sec07-card-f13.expected_back: The handbook warns that sixty miles per hour is too fast for visibility when the driver cannot see at least four hundred feet ahead.

sec07-card-f14.front: When may even thirty miles per hour be too fast for available visibility?
sec07-card-f14.expected_back: The handbook cautions that thirty miles per hour may be unsafe when the visible distance is less than one hundred fifty feet.

sec07-card-f15.front: Where is scanning sideways for entering vehicles and walkers most critical?
sec07-card-f15.expected_back: Search sideways for vehicles and pedestrians entering the path, especially at intersections and railroad crossings.

sec07-card-f16.front: Which everyday access points count as intersections besides street-to-street corners?
sec07-card-f16.expected_back: Intersections include driveways, shopping-center lanes and parking-lot entrances as well as crossing streets.

sec07-card-f17.front: Which five elements should you scan as you roll toward any intersection?
sec07-card-f17.expected_back: On intersection approach, check traffic, road users, controls, blocked views and pavement conditions.

sec07-card-f18.front: In what order should you look before entering an intersection and right after stopping?
sec07-card-f18.expected_back: Before entering an intersection, search ahead, left and right; after stopping, look left, right and left again.

sec07-card-f19.front: Why must you scan cross traffic right after your light turns green even though cross cars face red?
sec07-card-f19.expected_back: Check cross traffic even when it faces red or a stop sign, particularly immediately after the light turns green.

sec07-card-f20.front: What two conditions must exist before you pull into an intersection?
sec07-card-f20.expected_back: Enter an intersection only with a clear path through it and a view of crossing traffic, so a stop will not block it.

sec07-card-f21.front: How should you proceed after stopping at an intersection where hedges or parked trucks block your view?
sec07-card-f21.expected_back: When stopped with a blocked cross-street view, edge forward slowly until the view opens.

sec07-card-f22.front: Which five roadside zones call for extra sideways scanning?
sec07-card-f22.expected_back: Give extra sideways attention near busy sidewalks, shopping areas, construction, playgrounds and schoolyards.

sec07-card-f23.front: What two things must you verify before starting a left turn across oncoming lanes?
sec07-card-f23.expected_back: Before a left turn across opposing traffic, find a safe gap and ensure vehicles or pedestrians will not block the turning path.

sec07-card-f24.front: Which three conflict sources must you check right before turning right?
sec07-card-f24.expected_back: Before turning right, check traffic from the left, opposing left-turners and crossing pedestrians.

sec07-card-f25.front: What should you do at the round rail warning, and what two rail hazards should you scan for?
sec07-card-f25.expected_back: At a railroad approach, slow at the round warning sign and look both ways for trains or maintenance equipment before the tracks.

sec07-card-f26.front: Why should you check your rearview mirrors more frequently in dense traffic?
sec07-card-f26.expected_back: Check behind more often in heavy traffic to detect tailgaters and vehicles approaching too fast.

sec07-card-f27.front: Before which four driving situations are mirror checks especially vital?
sec07-card-f27.expected_back: Rearward checks are particularly important before changing lanes, slowing, joining traffic or descending a long or steep hill.

sec07-card-f28.front: Which other vehicles must you scan for before moving into a target lane or merge space?
sec07-card-f28.expected_back: Before a lane change or merge, check behind and in the target lane, including vehicles already entering it or preparing to pass.

sec07-card-f29.front: What spacing must you protect ahead while glancing at mirrors for a lane change?
sec07-card-f29.expected_back: Maintain safe following space while checking mirrors for a lane change.

sec07-card-f30.front: What is a vehicle blind spot, and how must you check it?
sec07-card-f30.expected_back: A blind spot is an area the mirrors do not show; look over the shoulder toward the intended movement to check it.

sec07-card-f31.front: Why should you use repeated brief glances rather than one long stare over your shoulder?
sec07-card-f31.expected_back: Use repeated short checks instead of one long sideways look because traffic ahead may stop while attention is elsewhere.

sec07-card-f32.front: What five-step sequence completes a clean lane change?
sec07-card-f32.expected_back: For a lane change, signal, recheck toward the move, adjust speed and steer into the lane, then cancel the signal.

sec07-card-f33.front: Where is checking your mirrors before slowing down most critical?
sec07-card-f33.expected_back: Check mirrors whenever slowing, especially suddenly or at a driveway or parking space where followers may not expect it.

sec07-card-f34.front: Which vehicles should you watch for in your mirrors on a long or steep downhill grade?
sec07-card-f34.expected_back: On a long or steep descent, watch mirrors for rapidly approaching vehicles, especially large trucks and buses.

sec07-card-f35.front: How does the Kansas handbook define perception distance?
sec07-card-f35.expected_back: Perception distance is the distance traveled from seeing a hazard until recognizing it under ideal conditions.

sec07-card-f36.front: Which three factors can lengthen or shorten your perception distance?
sec07-card-f36.expected_back: Visibility, the hazard and a driver's mental or physical condition can change perception distance.

sec07-card-f37.front: What is an alert driver's average perception time according to the handbook?
sec07-card-f37.expected_back: The handbook gives an alert driver's average perception time as three quarters of a second to one second.

sec07-card-f38.front: What travel interval does reaction distance measure?
sec07-card-f38.expected_back: Reaction distance is the ideal-condition distance traveled before physically applying the brakes in response to a recognized hazard.

sec07-card-f39.front: How long is average reaction time, and about how far does a car travel during it at fifty mph?
sec07-card-f39.expected_back: The handbook gives average reaction time as three quarters of a second to one second and illustrates about fifty-five feet traveled at fifty miles per hour

sec07-card-f40.front: What part of a stop does braking distance measure?
sec07-card-f40.expected_back: Braking distance is the distance traveled while the brakes are being applied under ideal conditions.

sec07-card-f41.front: About how many feet of braking distance does the handbook's fifty-mph dry-road example take?
sec07-card-f41.expected_back: The handbook's fifty miles per hour dry-road example with good brakes gives about one hundred fifty-eight feet of braking distance.

sec07-card-f42.front: Which three distances add together to form total stopping distance?
sec07-card-f42.expected_back: Total stopping distance combines perception, reaction and braking travel until the vehicle fully stops.

sec07-card-f43.front: What minimum total stopping distance does the handbook give at fifty miles per hour under ideal conditions?
sec07-card-f43.expected_back: For its ideal-condition fifty miles per hour example, the handbook gives a minimum total stopping distance of two hundred sixty-eight feet.

sec07-card-f44.front: Compared with twenty miles per hour, how much impact force and braking distance occur at forty?
sec07-card-f44.expected_back: The handbook compares forty miles per hour with twenty miles per hour as four times the impact and braking distance, illustrating the effect of increased speed.

sec07-card-f45.front: Compared with twenty miles per hour, how much impact force and braking distance occur at sixty?
sec07-card-f45.expected_back: Its sixty miles per hour comparison with twenty miles per hour gives nine times the impact and braking distance.

sec07-card-f46.front: Compared with twenty miles per hour, how much impact force and braking distance occur at eighty?
sec07-card-f46.expected_back: Its eighty miles per hour comparison with twenty miles per hour gives sixteen times the impact and braking distance.

sec07-card-f47.front: How does slamming on the brakes abruptly affect drivers behind you?
sec07-card-f47.expected_back: Sudden slowing makes it harder for following vehicles to avoid a collision.

sec07-card-f48.front: How far ahead does the handbook advise searching to avoid last-second panic stops?
sec07-card-f48.expected_back: To avoid panic stops, the handbook recommends searching at least ten seconds ahead and making needed changes early.

sec07-card-f49.front: Beyond safety, what practical wallet benefit comes from planning ahead and slowing gradually?
sec07-card-f49.expected_back: Planning ahead and slowing gradually can conserve fuel.

sec07-card-f50.front: Which four factors must guide the speed you choose at any moment?
sec07-card-f50.expected_back: Choose speed for traffic and road conditions, available forward view, following space and applicable limits.

sec07-card-f51.front: For which three roadway situations does the handbook specifically call for lower speed?
sec07-card-f51.expected_back: Reduce speed before sharp curves, on slippery pavement and when animals may be on the road.

sec07-card-f52.front: When should you slow down for a curve, and why is hard braking mid-curve risky?
sec07-card-f52.expected_back: Slow to a safe speed before a curve rather than braking hard after entry, which can cause loss of traction.

sec07-card-f53.front: Which three conditions require trimming curve-entry speed even further?
sec07-card-f53.expected_back: Reduce curve-entry speed further when traction is poor, when following another vehicle or when the curve's end is hidden.

sec07-card-f54.front: Once you enter a curve at a safe speed, how should you use the accelerator?
sec07-card-f54.expected_back: At a safe curve speed, the handbook calls for slight, steady acceleration through the curve.

sec07-card-f55.front: Why must you slow down at the very first drops of rain, snow, or sleet?
sec07-card-f55.expected_back: Slow at the first signs of rain, snow or sleet because water mixes with dirt and oil to make the surface slippery.

sec07-card-f56.front: When is a sudden rainstorm on hot pavement at its slickest?
sec07-card-f56.expected_back: A sudden rain on hot pavement may be particularly slippery during the first few minutes before surface oil washes away.

sec07-card-f57.front: What two vehicle-control penalties come from reduced tire grip on wet pavement?
sec07-card-f57.expected_back: Poor grip on wet pavement lengthens stops and makes skid-free turning harder.

sec07-card-f58.front: By about how much does the Kansas handbook recommend dropping speed on wet roads?
sec07-card-f58.expected_back: For wet roads, the handbook recommends about ten miles per hour below the recommended speed to allow extra stopping and steering space.

sec07-card-f59.front: How much should you cut your speed when driving on packed snow?
sec07-card-f59.expected_back: For packed snow, the handbook recommends reducing speed by at least half.

sec07-card-f60.front: How should you handle speed on icy roads, and what is the safest choice overall?
sec07-card-f60.expected_back: On ice, reduce speed to provide extra stopping and recovery room; avoid driving on ice-covered roads if possible.

sec07-card-f61.front: Between which calendar dates does Kansas permit studded snow tires?
sec07-card-f61.expected_back: The handbook permits studded snow tires in Kansas from November one through April one.

sec07-card-f62.front: Where can a road's center crown and drainage slope pull a skidding vehicle?
sec07-card-f62.expected_back: A road's crown and drainage slope can carry a skidding vehicle toward the roadside.

sec07-card-f63.front: How does shaded pavement behave compared with sunny asphalt on cold, wet days?
sec07-card-f63.expected_back: Shaded pavement on cold wet days can freeze before other areas and dry later.

sec07-card-f64.front: Which elevated or sheltered road structures can ice over while regular roads stay clear?
sec07-card-f64.expected_back: Bridge, overpass and underpass pavement may be icy even when nearby roads are clear.

sec07-card-f65.front: Why is ice near thirty-two degrees often slicker than ice in deep sub-zero cold?
sec07-card-f65.expected_back: Near freezing, liquid water over ice can make the surface more slippery than ice at much colder temperatures.

sec07-card-f66.front: What happens between your tires and the road during hydroplaning?
sec07-card-f66.expected_back: Hydroplaning occurs when tires ride on pooled water and lose contact with the pavement.

sec07-card-f67.front: What is your primary defense against hydroplaning in rain or standing puddles?
sec07-card-f67.expected_back: Slow in rain and on wet roads with puddles to reduce hydroplaning risk.

sec07-card-f68.front: What conflict comes from driving faster than surrounding traffic, and what pace should you keep?
sec07-card-f68.expected_back: Driving faster than the traffic stream creates repeated passing conflicts; keep pace within legal limits.

sec07-card-f69.front: Driving more than how many miles per hour below traffic flow triggers dangerous bunching and passes?
sec07-card-f69.expected_back: The handbook warns that driving over fifteen miles per hour below the traffic stream can create dangerous bunching and passing attempts.

sec07-card-f70.front: What should a slow-moving driver do when traffic bunches up behind?
sec07-card-f70.expected_back: If traffic bunches behind a slow vehicle, its driver should pull over when safe and let others pass.

sec07-card-f71.front: Which two kinds of signs must you check and obey on a highway entrance ramp?
sec07-card-f71.expected_back: On an entrance ramp, check destination and route signs and obey ramp-speed signs.

sec07-card-f72.front: How should you use a highway acceleration lane before merging onto the main roadway?
sec07-card-f72.expected_back: Use an acceleration lane to approach traffic speed before joining the main roadway.

sec07-card-f73.front: How should you adjust in an acceleration lane if no merge gap opens right away?
sec07-card-f73.expected_back: Avoid reaching the end of an acceleration lane and stopping; if a gap is unavailable, slow within the lane while waiting.

sec07-card-f74.front: What painted line must you avoid crossing while merging from an acceleration lane?
sec07-card-f74.expected_back: Do not cross the solid white boundary when joining from an acceleration lane.

sec07-card-f75.front: Which checks and signal steps complete a safe merge onto a main highway?
sec07-card-f75.expected_back: Before joining the roadway, check mirrors and over the shoulder toward the move; signal and enter carefully when a gap opens.

sec07-card-f76.front: How far ahead of your exit does the handbook advise entering the exit lane in heavy traffic?
sec07-card-f76.expected_back: In heavy traffic, the handbook recommends reaching the exit lane about half a mile before the exit.

sec07-card-f77.front: Where should you start slowing down when your highway exit has a deceleration lane?
sec07-card-f77.expected_back: For an exit with a deceleration lane, maintain speed on the main roadway and reduce it after entering that lane.

sec07-card-f78.front: What three things must you account for when slowing onto a limited-access exit ramp?
sec07-card-f78.expected_back: When exiting a limited-access road, check the ramp speed and following traffic before slowing, and brake with regard to vehicles ahead.

sec07-card-f79.front: How should you adjust speed in cramped zones like shopping centers and busy downtown blocks?
sec07-card-f79.expected_back: Reduce speed in crowded places where maneuvering room is limited, including shopping areas and busy downtown streets.

sec07-card-f80.front: Why do rush-hour congestion, narrow bridges, tunnels, and toll plazas call for lower speed?
sec07-card-f80.expected_back: Heavy rush-hour traffic, narrow bridges, tunnels and toll plazas can require lower speed for limited space and changing movements.

sec07-card-f81.front: What sudden hazard must you stay alert for near schools, playgrounds, and neighborhood streets?
sec07-card-f81.expected_back: Near schools, playgrounds and residential streets, watch for children entering the road unexpectedly.

sec07-card-f82.front: Besides trains and exit room, what surface feature at railroad crossings may require slowing down?
sec07-card-f82.expected_back: At railroad crossings, check for trains and room to clear; uneven crossing levels may require slowing.

sec07-card-f83.front: What two penalties does excess speed impose on steering and reaction?
sec07-card-f83.expected_back: Excess speed reduces maneuvering ability and increases the distance traveled while reacting.

sec07-card-f84.front: How does higher speed affect roadside barriers and crash outcomes?
sec07-card-f84.expected_back: Higher speed can reduce barrier protection and increase collision severity.

sec07-card-f85.front: Which three extra risks—mechanical, personal, and traffic—does the handbook tie to high speed?
sec07-card-f85.expected_back: The handbook identifies added tire and brake wear, driver fatigue and harder distance judgments by others as speed-related risks.

sec07-card-f86.front: What speed limit does the Kansas handbook give for an urban district when no different limit is posted?
sec07-card-f86.expected_back: For normal conditions without special hazards or a different posted limit, the handbook gives thirty miles per hour for an urban district.

sec07-card-f100.front: What minimum following interval does Kansas specify, and how do unusual weather or traffic change it?
sec07-card-f100.expected_back: The handbook specifies a two-second minimum following interval, adding a second for unusual traffic or weather conditions.

sec07-card-f87.front: What road conditions do posted speed limits assume, and when must you drive below them?
sec07-card-f87.expected_back: A posted speed assumes ideal conditions; slow for wet or icy pavement, poor visibility or heavy traffic.

sec07-card-f88.front: Does a posted fifty-five-mph sign make fifty-five appropriate during a snowstorm?
sec07-card-f88.expected_back: A posted fifty-five miles per hour limit does not make fifty-five miles per hour appropriate during a snowstorm.

sec07-card-f89.front: When is checking your speedometer frequently especially important?
sec07-card-f89.expected_back: Check the speedometer frequently, especially after moving from a fast multilane road to a slower road.

sec07-card-f90.front: Which three driving habits lower rollover risk in high-center-of-gravity vehicles?
sec07-card-f90.expected_back: High-center-of-gravity vehicles are more prone to rollover; drive at a suitable lower speed, avoid abrupt direction changes and slow before curves.

sec07-card-f91.front: What does ABS stand for, and what is it engineered to let a driver do?
sec07-card-f91.expected_back: ABS means Anti-Lock Braking System and is intended to permit steering while braking without upsetting vehicle balance.

sec07-card-f92.front: How does ABS affect stopping distance on dry roads compared with wet surfaces?
sec07-card-f92.expected_back: ABS does not necessarily shorten dry-road stops, though the handbook says it generally shortens wet-surface stops.

sec07-card-f93.front: What three actions does the handbook direct when using ABS in an emergency?
sec07-card-f93.expected_back: For ABS use, the handbook directs the driver to find open space, press the brake firmly and steer toward that space.

sec07-card-f94.front: How should you confirm whether an unfamiliar vehicle is equipped with anti-lock brakes?
sec07-card-f94.expected_back: Use the owner's manual to establish whether a vehicle has ABS.

sec07-card-f95.front: How does the dashboard ABS light behave normally at startup versus during a fault?
sec07-card-f95.expected_back: The ABS indicator normally illuminates at startup and then goes out; a light that stays on indicates a malfunction.

sec07-card-f96.front: What does ESP stand for, and what two signals does it continuously compare?
sec07-card-f96.expected_back: ESP means Electronic Stability Program; it compares the driver's steering request with the vehicle's actual movement.

sec07-card-f97.front: What mechanical action can ESP take when it senses a traction mismatch?
sec07-card-f97.expected_back: ESP can apply individual brakes when it detects a traction-related mismatch to help reduce skidding.

sec07-card-f98.front: How should you steer during traction loss in an ESP-equipped vehicle?
sec07-card-f98.expected_back: During traction loss with ESP, steer toward the intended path and avoid abrupt steering.

sec07-card-f99.front: What core advantage does keeping an open space cushion around your car provide?
sec07-card-f99.expected_back: A space cushion gives more time to react to other road users.

sec07-card-f101.front: How do you count following time with a roadside marker, and what count is too close?
sec07-card-f101.expected_back: Check following time by counting from when the vehicle ahead clears a fixed marker until the following vehicle reaches it; fewer than two seconds is too close.

sec07-card-f102.front: What should you do if your fixed-marker count comes up shorter than two seconds?
sec07-card-f102.expected_back: If following too closely, slow down and repeat the fixed-marker count until the interval is at least two seconds.

sec07-card-f103.front: How do slippery road conditions change the basic two-second following rule?
sec07-card-f103.expected_back: Slippery roads may require more than the basic two-second following interval.

sec07-card-f104.front: How can you help a trailing driver who pulls out to overtake your vehicle?
sec07-card-f104.expected_back: When a following driver wants to pass, slow to create more room ahead and shorten the passing maneuver.

sec07-card-f105.front: What two hazards require leaving extra following space behind a motorcycle?
sec07-card-f105.expected_back: Leave extra space behind motorcycles for differing braking performance or a fallen rider.

sec07-card-f106.front: What two visibility wins come from dropping farther back behind a boxy van or truck?
sec07-card-f106.expected_back: Increase following space behind vehicles with blocked rear views so their drivers can see the following vehicle and its driver can see ahead.

sec07-card-f107.front: Why must you keep a bigger front cushion when hauling heavy cargo or towing a trailer?
sec07-card-f107.expected_back: Carry a larger front cushion when hauling a heavy load or towing a trailer because stopping takes longer and steering ability decreases.

sec07-card-f108.front: How should darkness or visibility-cutting weather change your following distance?
sec07-card-f108.expected_back: Increase following space in darkness or bad weather that reduces the forward view.

sec07-card-f109.front: How should you adjust the space in front of you when someone tailgates from behind?
sec07-card-f109.expected_back: When tailgated, increase the space ahead so braking or steering can be less abrupt.

sec07-card-f110.front: How should you adjust following space behind emergency vehicles?
sec07-card-f110.expected_back: Give emergency vehicles additional following space to operate.

sec07-card-f111.front: Behind which vehicles must you keep extra room near railroad tracks because they are required to stop?
sec07-card-f111.expected_back: Leave extra room behind vehicles that must stop at railroad crossings, such as buses and hazardous-material carriers.

sec07-card-f112.front: Why must you stop farther back behind another vehicle on an uphill grade?
sec07-card-f112.expected_back: Leave extra space when stopped behind another vehicle on an incline because it may roll backward before moving ahead.

sec07-card-f113.front: Which three habits of yours help a driver behind you maintain a safe following gap?
sec07-card-f113.expected_back: Steady speed, early signals and extra front space before slowing can help a following driver maintain a safe gap.

sec07-card-r01.front: What is the easiest move when you are being tailgated and an adjacent lane is open?
sec07-card-r01.expected_back: When tailgated and an empty lane is available, move into it to let the other vehicle pass.

sec07-card-r02.front: How should you handle a tailgater when no empty lane exists to move into?
sec07-card-r02.expected_back: If tailgated without an empty lane, wait for a clear road ahead and then slow gradually to encourage a pass.

sec07-card-r03.front: Why must you never tap or slam your brakes sharply to warn off a tailgater?
sec07-card-r03.expected_back: Do not brake sharply to discourage a tailgater; it raises rear-end and aggressive-driving risks.

sec07-card-r04.front: How many extra seconds should you add to your front following interval when being tailgated?
sec07-card-r04.expected_back: The handbook recommends adding two to three seconds to the front following interval when being followed too closely.

sec07-card-r05.front: How should you manage your speed instead of cruising right beside another car on a multilane road?
sec07-card-r05.expected_back: Avoid staying beside another vehicle on a multilane road; adjust speed to preserve lateral room.

sec07-card-r06.front: Where inside your lane should you normally track on a two-way road?
sec07-card-r06.expected_back: On a two-way road, avoid crowding the centerline; the lane center generally leaves room to evade either way.

sec07-card-r07.front: How can you help ramp traffic merge smoothly onto a multilane highway?
sec07-card-r07.expected_back: Make room for merging traffic by moving to the next lane when that lane is clear.

sec07-card-r08.front: How should you position past parked cars without crossing the centerline?
sec07-card-r08.expected_back: Leave extra room beside parked cars without crossing the centerline because doors, people or vehicles may enter the path.

sec07-card-r09.front: Which vulnerable road users especially need extra lateral space for sudden movements?
sec07-card-r09.expected_back: Give pedestrians and cyclists, particularly children, additional space for unexpected movement.

sec07-card-r10.front: Where inside your lane can you ease while a tractor-trailer overtakes you?
sec07-card-r10.expected_back: When a tractor-trailer passes, moving toward the outside of the lane can increase separation while remaining within the lane.

sec07-card-r11.front: How big should a merge opening be before you pull into moving traffic?
sec07-card-r11.expected_back: Select a merge gap that leaves time to establish a suitable following interval rather than forcing into a small opening.

sec07-card-r12.front: How must you cross several lanes on a wide roadway, and why?
sec07-card-r12.expected_back: Cross multiple lanes one at a time because checking several at once is difficult and can create conflicts.

sec07-card-r13.front: From a stop under normal conditions, about how many seconds does crossing straight across an intersection take?
sec07-card-r13.expected_back: After stopping before crossing traffic, allow enough gap to get fully across; the handbook's normal-condition example is about three to five seconds.

sec07-card-r14.front: What two phases must your traffic gap cover when turning onto a moving street?
sec07-card-r14.expected_back: When entering traffic with a turn, allow room both to complete the turn and to accelerate.

sec07-card-r15.front: About how many seconds does the handbook's normal right-turn-and-acceleration example take?
sec07-card-r15.expected_back: The handbook's normal-condition right-turn-and-acceleration example takes about twelve to fifteen seconds.

sec07-card-r16.front: About how many seconds does the handbook's normal left-turn-and-acceleration example require?
sec07-card-r16.expected_back: Its normal-condition left-turn-and-acceleration example takes about fifteen to eighteen seconds.

sec07-card-r17.front: May you start across an intersection on a green light when traffic blocks the exit side?
sec07-card-r17.expected_back: Do not begin crossing even on green if vehicles block the exit path.

sec07-card-r18.front: Before starting a left turn, what must you confirm will not trap you across oncoming lanes?
sec07-card-r18.expected_back: Before a left turn, confirm that neither vehicles nor pedestrians will trap the vehicle in the opposing path.

sec07-card-r19.front: Why must you wait before pulling out in front of an approaching car whose turn signal is flashing?
sec07-card-r19.expected_back: Do not enter merely because another driver's turn signal is on; wait for the turn to begin and a genuinely safe gap.

sec07-card-r20.front: What two harmless mistakes explain why an approaching car's blinker might flash past your corner?
sec07-card-r20.expected_back: Another vehicle's signal may indicate a later turn or may have been left on accidentally, especially if it does not self-cancel.

sec07-card-r21.front: When is it safe to start driving onto railroad tracks?
sec07-card-r21.expected_back: Cross railroad tracks only when there is room to clear without stopping on them.

sec07-card-r22.front: Why should you complete an overtaking pass promptly within safe limits?
sec07-card-r22.expected_back: Complete a pass as promptly as safety permits to limit time beside another vehicle.

sec07-card-r23.front: Which forward and rearward zones must you check before starting to pass?
sec07-card-r23.expected_back: Before passing, check oncoming traffic, side-road entries and slowing vehicles ahead, as well as mirrors and the rear blind spot.

sec07-card-r24.front: From how far behind the lead car should you signal and begin a pass?
sec07-card-r24.memory_hook: Signal at least two seconds back
sec07-card-r24.expected_back: Signal a safe pass and begin from at least two seconds behind the vehicle being overtaken.

sec07-card-r25.front: How should you steer and scan while alongside the vehicle you are passing?
sec07-card-r25.expected_back: Steer smoothly into the passing lane, keep checking ahead and in mirrors, and avoid drifting toward the passed vehicle.

sec07-card-r26.front: What rearview mirror cue tells you it is safe to signal and return to your lane after passing?
sec07-card-r26.expected_back: Before returning after a pass, see the entire front of the passed vehicle in the rearview mirror, then signal and return smoothly.

sec07-card-r27.front: How should you position and pace your car while another driver overtakes you?
sec07-card-r27.expected_back: When being passed, move toward the right side of the lane and maintain a steady speed.

sec07-card-r28.front: Does a broken yellow line or passing-zone sign guarantee it is safe to pass?
sec07-card-r28.expected_back: Passing permission from signs or markings still requires enough safe space.

sec07-card-r29.front: How many vehicles should you pass at once, and how long warns the handbook a pass can take?
sec07-card-r29.expected_back: The handbook recommends passing one vehicle at a time and warns that a pass can take as long as twenty to thirty seconds.

sec07-card-r30.front: What is the rule if you can see an oncoming vehicle or feel unsure about passing distance?
sec07-card-r30.expected_back: Do not attempt a pass when an oncoming vehicle is visible; if time or distance is uncertain, wait.

sec07-card-r31.front: Why is judging passing distance against oncoming traffic naturally tricky for human eyes?
sec07-card-r31.expected_back: Oncoming vehicles can appear slower than their actual closing speed, making passing-distance judgment difficult.

sec07-card-r32.front: What does it mean if you can actually see an oncoming vehicle getting closer ahead?
sec07-card-r32.expected_back: The handbook's perception warning says a vehicle more than twenty-five seconds away may look stationary; visible closing motion may mean less than twenty-five seconds remains.

sec07-card-r33.front: At fifty-five to sixty mph, how much clear forward view is needed to pass near hills or curves?
sec07-card-r33.expected_back: For passing near hills or curves at fifty-five to sixty miles per hour, the handbook calls for at least one-third mile of forward view, about twenty to twenty-five seconds.

sec07-card-r34.front: How must you treat any hill or curve blocking sight, and how close may no pass start?
sec07-card-r34.expected_back: Treat a hill or curve that blocks the view as hiding opposing traffic and do not start passing within one-third mile of it.

sec07-card-r35.front: At which roadway junctions and side-access points must you avoid passing?
sec07-card-r35.expected_back: Do not pass in intersections, and avoid passing at other crossing points such as driveways, alleys or parking entrances.

sec07-card-r36.front: Which roadside hazards ahead could suddenly force the car you are passing sideways into you?
sec07-card-r36.expected_back: Before a pass, look for pedestrians, cyclists, narrow bridges, ice, potholes or obstructions that may force another vehicle sideways.

sec07-card-r37.front: What return-space rule governs passing a vehicle inside a line of traffic?
sec07-card-r37.expected_back: Do not pass without room to return to the travel lane, and do not depend on other drivers creating that room.

sec07-card-r38.front: Within how many seconds of travel before a railroad crossing does the handbook advise against passing?
sec07-card-r38.expected_back: The handbook advises against passing with a railroad crossing in the next twenty to twenty-five seconds of travel.

sec07-card-r39.front: Which two kinds of entering drivers need extra space because they cannot see you well?
sec07-card-r39.expected_back: Allow extra space for drivers whose view is blocked at intersections or driveways and for drivers backing into the road.

sec07-card-r40.front: What everyday weather gear or window issue warns you someone cannot see traffic clearly?
sec07-card-r40.expected_back: Give extra room to people whose vision is obstructed by icy windows, umbrellas or lowered hats.

sec07-card-r41.front: Around which busy or preoccupied groups should you add extra caution and buffer space?
sec07-card-r41.expected_back: Use additional caution or space around distracted people such as delivery workers, construction workers and inattentive pedestrians.

sec07-card-r42.front: What erratic moves signal a confused driver hunting for an address or turn?
sec07-card-r42.expected_back: Allow for confused drivers who slow unexpectedly or search for directions or addresses.

sec07-card-r43.front: What should you do if an overtaking driver misjudges oncoming traffic and runs low on room?
sec07-card-r43.expected_back: If a passing driver runs short of space, slow down to help that vehicle return safely.

sec07-card-r44.front: How should you respond when another driver needs an abrupt lane change right ahead of you?
sec07-card-r44.expected_back: If another driver needs an abrupt lane change, slowing to let that driver merge can reduce conflict.

sec07-card-r45.front: How do you separate hazards when an oncoming car and a roadside walker line up ahead?
sec07-card-r45.expected_back: Handle hazards separately when possible; delay passing a roadside pedestrian until an opposing vehicle has gone by.

sec07-card-r46.front: What is the main safety payoff of signaling your position and next move clearly?
sec07-card-r46.expected_back: Communicating location and intended movement helps other road users anticipate the vehicle's actions.

sec07-card-r47.front: Why should you switch on headlights whenever rain, snow, or fog cuts visibility?
sec07-card-r47.expected_back: Use headlights to improve the vehicle's visibility to others, especially when rain, snow or fog reduces visibility.

sec07-card-r48.front: When does Kansas law require your headlights to be turned on during wet weather?
sec07-card-r48.expected_back: The handbook states that Kansas requires headlights whenever the vehicle's wipers are used.

sec07-card-r49.front: When as evening approaches should you switch your headlights on?
sec07-card-r49.expected_back: Switch on headlights as daylight fades; doing so slightly early helps other drivers see the vehicle.

sec07-card-r50.front: Why should you turn headlights on when driving away from a low rising or setting sun?
sec07-card-r50.expected_back: Use headlights while driving away from a low rising or setting sun to help opposing drivers see the vehicle.

sec07-card-r51.front: What three upkeep steps keep headlights effective without blinding oncoming drivers?
sec07-card-r51.expected_back: Keep headlights clean and working and have a qualified person check their aim to preserve visibility without dazzling others.

sec07-card-r52.front: For what legitimate safety purpose is a vehicle's horn designed?
sec07-card-r52.expected_back: A horn can warn of an imminent collision, including a pedestrian entering the street or vehicles about to strike one another.

sec07-card-r53.front: Which three everyday horn uses does the Kansas handbook tell drivers to avoid?
sec07-card-r53.expected_back: Do not use the horn to greet someone, complain about an error or pressure a driver to move faster.

sec07-card-r54.front: How should you use your horn around a blind pedestrian?
sec07-card-r54.expected_back: Avoid sounding the horn near a blind pedestrian.

sec07-card-r55.front: Who should you notify if possible during a roadside breakdown, and where might a number appear?
sec07-card-r55.expected_back: If possible during a breakdown, notify authorities by phone or another device; roadside signs may give an emergency number.

sec07-card-r56.front: Where should you guide your vehicle as soon as a breakdown forces a stop?
sec07-card-r56.expected_back: For a breakdown stop, move away from traffic and off the road when possible.

sec07-card-r57.front: Which vehicle lights must you switch on immediately to mark a disabled car?
sec07-card-r57.expected_back: Turn on hazard flashers to indicate a disabled vehicle.

sec07-card-r58.front: Which two blind spots on a road must you avoid stopping just beyond during a breakdown?
sec07-card-r58.expected_back: Choose a breakdown stopping place visible to approaching users rather than just beyond a hillcrest or bend.

sec07-card-r59.front: About how far behind a disabled vehicle does the handbook place roadside warning flares?
sec07-card-r59.expected_back: The handbook describes placing warning flares about two hundred to three hundred feet behind a disabled vehicle to alert approaching drivers.

sec07-card-r60.front: What two dangerous breakdown actions inside a live traffic lane must you never attempt?
sec07-card-r60.expected_back: Do not remain in the roadway or attempt a tire change within a traffic lane.

sec07-card-r61.front: Which non-electric signals show passing patrols that your parked car is disabled?
sec07-card-r61.expected_back: A white cloth on the antenna, mirror or door handle, or a raised hood, can indicate a disabled vehicle.

sec07-card-r62.front: Which two kinds of vehicle changes require signaling to surrounding road users?
sec07-card-r62.expected_back: Signal changes in direction or slowing so other road users can anticipate the movement.

sec07-card-r63.front: How does the handbook match turn-signal modes to intersection turns versus lane shifts?
sec07-card-r63.expected_back: Use turn signals before intersection turns and the lane-change signal function for lane changes or merges.

sec07-card-r64.front: What check should follow every completed turn or gentle lane change?
sec07-card-r64.expected_back: After a turn or lane change, check that the signal has canceled and switch it off if necessary.

sec07-card-r65.front: How do brake lights communicate with traffic behind, and when should you begin slowing?
sec07-card-r65.expected_back: Brake lights communicate slowing; reduce speed as early as safely possible.

sec07-card-r66.front: How many light brake-pedal taps does the handbook recommend before an unexpected slowdown?
sec07-card-r66.expected_back: When slowing unexpectedly, the handbook recommends three or four light brake-pedal taps to warn following traffic.

sec07-card-r67.front: When turning off a fast road that lacks a dedicated turn or exit lane, what must come first?
sec07-card-r67.expected_back: Warn before slowing to turn off a road without a separate exit or turn lane.

sec07-card-r68.front: Why must you warn early before parking or turning into a driveway just ahead of an intersection?
sec07-card-r68.expected_back: Warn before parking or turning before an intersection when followers may expect continued travel through it.

sec07-card-r69.front: Why is extra brake-light warning vital when slowing for a hazard or queue with a close follower?
sec07-card-r69.expected_back: Warn before slowing for a hidden hazard or traffic queue that a close follower cannot see.

sec07-card-r70.front: How does Kansas classify holding a driver's license?
sec07-card-r70.expected_back: A driver's license is a privilege rather than a right.

sec07-card-r71.front: In what personal condition must you always operate a motor vehicle?
sec07-card-r71.expected_back: Drive without drug, alcohol or other impairment.

sec07-card-r72.front: Who inside a moving vehicle should wear a seat belt?
sec07-card-r72.expected_back: The driver and passengers should always wear seat belts.

sec07-card-r73.front: Who shares financial responsibility for damages caused by a minor's driving?
sec07-card-r73.expected_back: A minor and the minor's parent or guardian bear financial consequences of the minor's driving.

sec07-card-r74.front: What two responsibilities stay on a driver whenever leaving a vehicle parked?
sec07-card-r74.expected_back: Drivers are responsible for parking without obstructing traffic or pedestrians and preventing the vehicle from rolling away.

sec07-card-r75.front: What everyday habit solves awkward traffic moments that written statutes do not explicitly cover?
sec07-card-r75.expected_back: Courtesy helps address situations that traffic rules do not explicitly cover.

sec07-card-r76.front: Which three categories of limitations and conditions must you evaluate as driving risks?
sec07-card-r76.expected_back: Assess personal driving limitations, vehicle limitations and road or weather conditions as sources of risk.

sec07-card-r77.front: How do built-in risk trade-offs differ between large vehicles and small vehicles?
sec07-card-r77.expected_back: Large vehicles may be less stable with restricted surrounding visibility, while small vehicles may be harder for others to see.

sec07-card-r78.front: How do you manage spotted driving risks, and can road risk ever reach zero?
sec07-card-r78.expected_back: Manage identified risks through position and speed changes; risks can be reduced but not completely eliminated.

sec07-card-r79.front: What three tactical gains come from timely speed or lane-position adjustments?
sec07-card-r79.expected_back: Position or speed changes can increase response time, improve control and separate conflicting hazards.

sec07-card-r80.front: What builds faster, cleaner driving decisions over time?
sec07-card-r80.expected_back: Driving decisions improve with practice and experience.

sec07-card-r81.front: With what active habit must every good driving decision begin?
sec07-card-r81.expected_back: Begin decisions with an active search for other users, their positions and their paths.

sec07-card-r82.front: Once your scan spots other road users, what should you evaluate next?
sec07-card-r82.expected_back: After identifying road users, assess their movement and whether they could collide with the vehicle.

sec07-card-r83.front: Which three response categories can execute your driving decision once chosen?
sec07-card-r83.expected_back: Responses can include changes in speed, changes in direction and communication; take action after choosing the response.

sec07-card-r84.front: What three-step mental loop should you practice continuously while driving?
sec07-card-r84.expected_back: Practice anticipating a possible hazard, deciding how to reduce its risk and then acting.

sec07-card-r85.front: How can asking yourself silent what-if questions while cruising improve emergency readiness?
sec07-card-r85.expected_back: Rehearsing possible situations with what-if questions can help prepare for rapid decisions.

sec08-card-f01.front: Which three driver actions can avoid a crash, and what determines which one to use?
sec08-card-f01.expected_back: Collision-avoidance responses include braking, steering or accelerating, depending on available space and the threat.

sec08-card-f02.front: Where should you look to learn the specific anti-lock braking instructions for your vehicle?
sec08-card-f02.expected_back: Read the vehicle owner's manual for its ABS instructions.

sec08-card-f03.front: How should you use the brake pedal when making an emergency stop with anti-lock brakes?
sec08-card-f03.expected_back: For a rapid stop with ABS, press the brake firmly and keep pressure on it.

sec08-card-f04.front: What should you do if an anti-lock brake pedal pushes back or pulses under your foot?
sec08-card-f04.expected_back: ABS operation may push back through the brake pedal; maintain pressure rather than lifting because of that feedback.

sec08-card-f05.front: What happens if you slam the brake pedal too hard in a vehicle without anti-lock brakes?
sec08-card-f05.expected_back: Without ABS, overly hard braking can lock the wheels and start a skid.

sec08-card-f06.front: How hard should you brake during a rapid stop in a vehicle that lacks anti-lock brakes?
sec08-card-f06.expected_back: For a rapid stop without ABS, apply as much braking as possible without locking the wheels.

sec08-card-f07.front: How do you recover if non-ABS brakes lock up during an emergency stop?
sec08-card-f07.expected_back: If non-ABS brakes lock, ease pedal pressure without removing the foot, then reapply controlled braking once the skid ends.

sec08-card-f08.front: How long should you continue easing and reapplying non-ABS brakes if lockup threatens again?
sec08-card-f08.expected_back: Repeat non-ABS release-and-reapply control as needed until stopped.

sec08-card-f09.front: Why can steering around a sudden hazard beat hitting the brakes in many emergencies?
sec08-card-f09.expected_back: Steering around a collision threat may be quicker than stopping in many situations.

sec08-card-f10.front: How should you hold the wheel and prepare during an emergency steering move?
sec08-card-f10.expected_back: Keep both hands firmly on the wheel during emergency steering and remain ready to control the vehicle after the avoidance move.

sec08-card-f11.front: Where must you aim when steering to escape an imminent collision?
sec08-card-f11.expected_back: Steer toward the intended path and avoid escaping one collision into another.

sec08-card-f12.front: How does wearing a seat belt help you control the car during a sharp emergency swerve?
sec08-card-f12.expected_back: A seat belt helps keep the driver in position behind the wheel during an emergency maneuver.

sec08-card-f13.front: How do you combine braking and steering during an emergency maneuver in an ABS-equipped car?
sec08-card-f13.expected_back: With ABS during an emergency steering maneuver, maintain firm brake pressure while steering toward the intended path.

sec08-card-f14.front: How should you manage the brakes while steering around a hazard without anti-lock brakes?
sec08-card-f14.expected_back: Without ABS, avoid hard braking while steering if possible; stronger braking can resume after reaching the intended path and straightening.

sec08-card-f15.front: When can pressing the accelerator help prevent a crash, and what comes right after?
sec08-card-f15.expected_back: Acceleration may avoid a side or rear strike when open space exists ahead; slow again after the danger passes.

sec08-card-f16.front: Which surface conditions and driver inputs commonly cause tires to lose grip?
sec08-card-f16.expected_back: Wet, snowy or icy surfaces, excessive speed and abrupt stopping can cause tires to lose their grip.

sec08-card-f17.front: Where should your eyes lock immediately when your tires start losing traction?
sec08-card-f17.expected_back: At the start of traction loss, look toward available open space rather than fixating on the hazard.

sec08-card-f18.front: What first pedal step helps you tell whether front or rear tires lost traction?
sec08-card-f18.expected_back: The handbook's skid-identification step releases accelerator or brake pressure to help determine whether front or rear traction is lost.

sec08-card-f19.front: Which tires have lost grip if turning the steering wheel fails to alter your straight-ahead path?
sec08-card-f19.expected_back: If steering does not change the vehicle's straight path, the front tires have lost traction.

sec08-card-f20.front: What tire condition is happening when the vehicle swings sideways without extra steering input?
sec08-card-f20.expected_back: Sideways movement without added steering input indicates rear-tire traction loss.

sec08-card-f21.front: How do you recover front-tire grip during a non-ABS skid?
sec08-card-f21.expected_back: For front traction loss in the described non-ABS response, ease braking to recover grip and reapply without skidding.

sec08-card-f22.front: What brake action does the Kansas handbook direct when front tires lose grip in an ABS vehicle?
sec08-card-f22.expected_back: For front traction loss with ABS, the handbook directs full brake application to regain steering control.

sec08-card-f23.front: How should you steer and aim your eyes to recover when rear tires slide sideways?
sec08-card-f23.expected_back: For rear traction loss, steer toward the desired path and countersteer as needed until straight, continuing to look toward that path.

sec08-card-f24.front: Why must you avoid glancing into the oncoming lane while recovering from a skid?
sec08-card-f24.expected_back: During skid recovery, avoid looking into the opposing lane because the vehicle may follow that gaze across the centerline.

sec08-card-f25.front: What should you keep doing with the wheel when traction-assistance tech activates during a rear skid?
sec08-card-f25.expected_back: With traction-assistance technology during rear traction loss, keep steering toward the desired path to assist the system.

sec08-card-f26.front: What single habit remains a primary defense against injury when a crash cannot be avoided?
sec08-card-f26.expected_back: If a collision cannot be avoided, seat-belt use is a key way to reduce resulting injury.

sec08-card-f27.front: How should you position your body and feet right before your car is struck from behind?
sec08-card-f27.expected_back: For a rear impact, press against the seat back with the head against its restraint and prepare to brake against being pushed into another vehicle.

sec08-card-f28.front: How do lap-and-shoulder belts help in a side crash, and what should you prepare to do?
sec08-card-f28.expected_back: Lap-and-shoulder belts help retain the driver behind the wheel in a side impact; prepare to steer or brake to avoid a subsequent collision.

sec08-card-f29.front: Why do seat belts remain crucial right after an initial frontal impact?
sec08-card-f29.expected_back: Seat belts help protect and retain the driver if a frontal crash is followed by another collision.

sec08-card-r01.front: What routine habit lowers the chance of dangerous mechanical failures on the road?
sec08-card-r01.expected_back: Follow the vehicle owner's recommended maintenance schedule to reduce mechanical-failure risk.

sec08-card-r02.front: What is the first pedal action the Kansas handbook recommends if your brakes stop working?
sec08-card-r02.expected_back: If the brakes actually stop working, the handbook first recommends several rapid pedal pumps, which may restore enough pressure to stop.

sec08-card-r03.front: How should you apply the parking brake if pumping failed service brakes restores no stopping power?
sec08-card-r03.expected_back: If pumping failed brakes does not work, use the described parking-brake handle or pedal gradually to avoid locking rear wheels.

sec08-card-r04.front: What must you stay ready to do if applying the parking brake during brake failure starts a rear skid?
sec08-card-r04.expected_back: If parking-brake application during brake failure starts a skid, be ready to release it.

sec08-card-r05.front: What must you do once off the road after losing your brakes completely?
sec08-card-r05.expected_back: If braking cannot be restored, seek a safe place off the roadway to slow and stop, and do not continue driving without functioning brakes.

sec08-card-r06.front: What is a tire blowout, and how does a front-tire blowout pull the vehicle?
sec08-card-r06.expected_back: A blowout is rapid tire deflation; a front blowout can pull the vehicle sharply toward that tire.

sec08-card-r07.front: How does a rear-tire blowout typically feel from the driver's seat?
sec08-card-r07.expected_back: A rear blowout can cause wobbling, shaking and some pull toward the failed tire.

sec08-card-r08.front: What is your immediate steering priority right after a blowout or sudden flat?
sec08-card-r08.expected_back: After a blowout or sudden flat, hold the wheel firmly and keep the vehicle straight.

sec08-card-r09.front: How should you shed speed right after a tire blows out?
sec08-card-r09.expected_back: For a blowout, release the accelerator and slow gradually; let the vehicle slow naturally, using gentle braking only if necessary.

sec08-card-r10.front: Where should you stop after a blowout, and what warning should you switch on?
sec08-card-r10.expected_back: After a blowout, avoid stopping on the road if possible; pull to a safe place, activate hazard flashers and arrange tire replacement.

sec08-card-r11.front: What happens to your steering if the engine shuts off while your vehicle is moving?
sec08-card-r11.expected_back: If the engine shuts off while moving, hold the wheel firmly; steering may require greater effort but remains possible.

sec08-card-r12.front: Which gear and braking style should you use to pull off the road after an engine stalls at speed?
sec08-card-r12.expected_back: After an engine shutdown, select neutral, seek an escape path and use steady braking rather than a hard application to pull off the road.

sec08-card-r13.front: What steps follow once you pull off and stop for a stalled engine that refuses to restart?
sec08-card-r13.expected_back: After stopping for engine shutdown, try restarting; if it fails, raise the hood, use hazard flashers and call for help.

sec08-card-r14.front: What two mechanical problems can cause accelerator failure?
sec08-card-r14.expected_back: Accelerator failure may result from a broken spring or a pedal stuck down.

sec08-card-r15.front: How do you safely bring the car off the road if the accelerator sticks down?
sec08-card-r15.expected_back: For accelerator failure, select neutral and seek an escape path, then steer smoothly and brake gently to leave the roadway.

sec08-card-r16.front: What must you do once safely stopped after an accelerator-failure incident?
sec08-card-r16.expected_back: After stopping for accelerator failure, switch off the vehicle and have the pedal repaired before driving again.

sec08-card-r17.front: Why must you resist yanking the wheel right back onto the road when tires drop off the pavement edge?
sec08-card-r17.expected_back: If wheels leave the pavement, avoid an immediate panic return because excessive steering before slowing can cause a serious crash.

sec08-card-r18.front: How should you manage pedals and steering immediately after dropping wheels off the pavement?
sec08-card-r18.expected_back: For a pavement drop-off, ease the accelerator, avoid hard braking and use gentle brakes while steering straight.

sec08-card-r19.front: Down to what speed does the Kansas handbook recommend slowing before steering back onto pavement?
sec08-card-r19.expected_back: The handbook recommends slowing to twenty-five miles per hour or less before its pavement-return maneuver.

sec08-card-r20.front: How does straddling the dropped pavement edge help before turning back onto the road?
sec08-card-r20.expected_back: Straddling the pavement edge can keep the tires' inside edges from rubbing and allow a better angle for returning.

sec08-card-r21.front: How much wheel input guides a low-speed pavement return once traffic is clear in every direction?
sec08-card-r21.expected_back: With traffic gaps in all directions, the described pavement return uses about a quarter-turn of the wheel; avoid oversteering and guide back into the lane after reaching pavement.

sec08-card-r22.front: What is the safest move after a drop-off when traffic is heavy and a wide shoulder is available?
sec08-card-r22.expected_back: If traffic is heavy and the shoulder is wide, move fully onto the shoulder and stop, then wait for a large gap before reentering.

sec08-card-r23.front: What should you do if slope or obstacles make returning to the pavement impossible?
sec08-card-r23.expected_back: If returning to pavement is not possible, stop as far from the road as possible and wait for help.

sec08-card-r24.front: What roadside features can trip a sideways-sliding vehicle into a rollover?
sec08-card-r24.expected_back: A sideways-sliding vehicle can trip over a curb, guardrail, stump or soft uneven ground and roll over.

sec08-card-r25.front: Which two driver inputs commonly trigger vehicle rollovers?
sec08-card-r25.expected_back: Excess speed or a sharp steering input can contribute to a rollover.

sec08-card-r26.front: How can a crash involving multiple vehicles trigger a rollover?
sec08-card-r26.expected_back: A multivehicle impact can also initiate a rollover through lost control or a side strike.

sec08-card-r27.front: Why are SUVs, vans, pickups, and small trucks more prone to rolling over than passenger sedans?
sec08-card-r27.expected_back: SUVs, vans, pickups and small trucks are more rollover-prone than passenger cars because of higher centers of gravity.

sec08-card-r28.front: How does adding passengers or heavy cargo affect a vehicle's rollover risk?
sec08-card-r28.expected_back: Additional passengers or cargo can increase rollover risk.

sec08-card-r29.front: How do moderated speed and extra bad-weather caution lower rollover risk?
sec08-card-r29.expected_back: Appropriate speed and added caution in bad weather can reduce rollover risk by leaving more response time.

sec08-card-r30.front: What steering mistake must you avoid at high speed, on soft ground, or after dropping off pavement?
sec08-card-r30.expected_back: Avoid abrupt steering at high speed or on soft surfaces; after leaving pavement, slow gradually instead of jerking back onto it.

sec08-card-r31.front: How do seat belts cut severe injury and death during a rollover crash?
sec08-card-r31.expected_back: Seat belts reduce rollover injury and ejection risk by keeping occupants in the vehicle.

sec08-card-r32.front: What two rollover hazards can rollover-sensing side airbags help reduce?
sec08-card-r32.expected_back: Rollover-sensing side airbags can help reduce upper-body ground contact and occupant ejection.

sec08-card-r33.front: What rule governs how fast you can safely drive at night?
sec08-card-r33.expected_back: At night, choose a speed that permits stopping within the distance illuminated and visible ahead.

sec08-card-r34.front: How much extra following time does the Kansas handbook add at night and on unfamiliar night roads?
sec08-card-r34.expected_back: For night driving, the handbook recommends adding at least one second to following space, or at least two seconds on unfamiliar roads at night.

sec08-card-r35.front: Above what speed does the handbook warn driving is unsafe when weather cuts forward sight to one hundred feet?
sec08-card-r35.expected_back: When rain, snow, dust, smoke or dense fog limits the forward view to one hundred feet, the handbook warns that speeds above thirty miles per hour are unsafe.
